Sources indicate that catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

It has been revealed that throughout October, we are throwing our support behind the mission to turn Feral Cat Day into Feral Cat Awareness Month, an opportunity to raise awareness about community cats (also called feral or stray), promote Trap-Neuter-Return, and recognize the millions of caring people who dedicate their time and energy to improving the lives of the cats & kittens most in need of support. With around 60-100 million stray cats in the US, we know it takes more than just one day to make a meaningful difference in a problem this overwhelming, and one group that understands this more than most is The Cat Network in Miami, Florida.

Founded in 1995, The Cat Network is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization supported by more than 2,500 volunteers and donors, helping community cats, stray, abandoned, and homeless cats throughout South Florida while supporting the people who care for them. Through education, low-cost spay/neuter services, adoption assistance, and advocacy, the organization works to humanely reduce cat overpopulation and improve the lives of cats and the communities they live in.

The Cat Network is dedicated to humanely reducing cat overpopulation in South Florida through five core pillars: education, sterilization, adoption, advocacy, and humane public policy. Our story begins more than 30 years agoâ¦.

Recent findings suggest that in July 1995, the City Manager of Miami Beach contracted with a commercial trapper, Humane Animal Removal, to trap and euthanize the cityâs feral cats, with a bounty of $35.00 for each cat trapped and killed. When this became public, a local and national outcry ensued, and the media had a field day. The Cat Network, still in its infancy, helped organize local opposition to the trap-kill strategy. Susan Fleming, president of The Cat Network and a Miami Beach resident, was instrumental in negotiating with the City to institute TNR instead. With help from Animal Controlâs mobile animal clinic and SoBe spay/neuter certificates, we convinced the City to implement the more humane approach of TNR.

It has been revealed that the following year, we began our spay/neuter certificate program with participating veterinary clinics, the first of which was Galloway Animal Clinic. Since 1995, we've helped sterilize more than 122,000 cats and assisted in the adoption of more than 24,000 cats.

Industry observers note that what makes us unique is our comprehensive approach. Rather than simply responding to the symptoms of overpopulation, we focus on preventing future litters while helping cats in need. Our programs include the Miami Meow Mobile, low-cost spay/neuter vouchers, adoption referrals through an extensive foster network, public education, and advocacy for Trap-Neuter-Return (TNR) as the most humane and effective way to manage community cat populations.

One of our biggest challenges is simply the sheer number of cats needing help. Because South Florida has warm weather year-round, kitten season never truly ends. This creates an ongoing demand for spay and neuter services, foster homes, adoptions, and community education. Every day we receive calls from residents who have discovered kittens, injured cats, or growing community cat colonies.

There really isn't an "off season" for cat rescue here, so our volunteers and veterinary programs stay busy throughout the entire year. Preventing unwanted litters through early sterilization is one of the most effective ways to reduce this constant cycle.

Recent findings suggest that funding is another ongoing challenge. Keeping our veterinary programs affordable requires significant community support, and the costs of medical supplies, equipment, and operations continue to rise.

People can make an enormous difference by:.

Donating to support our programs.

Becoming a volunteer or foster caregiver.

Spaying and neutering their own pets.

Helping community cats through TNR.

Sharing our educational resources and adoptable cats on social media.

Becoming a member of The Cat Network.

Every donation, volunteer hour, and shared post helps save lives.

According to recent reports, over the past 30 years, The Cat Network has become one of South Florida's leading organizations dedicated to reducing cat overpopulation. Sterilizing more than 122,000 cats and helping over 24,000 cats find homes are milestones that represent countless lives saved.

According to recent reports, we're especially proud of the Miami Meow Mobile, which has dramatically increased access to affordable veterinary care, and our long-standing network of volunteers and foster caregivers who make our adoption program possible. Together, these programs have helped thousands of residents become part of the solution while improving animal welfare throughout South Florida.

Recent findings suggest that the Miami Meow Mobile is a fully equipped veterinary clinic designed specifically for cats. Originally envisioned in 2001 and launched in 2005, it was created to make affordable veterinary care accessible to more people throughout the community.

Today, the Meow Mobile provides low-cost spay and neuter surgeries, vaccinations, testing, microchipping, parasite treatments, and basic wellness services. Originally designed as a traveling clinic, it presently operates from a fixed location in Kendall, allowing us to serve a large number of cats efficiently and safely.

The Meow Mobile remains one of our signature programs because every surgery performed helps prevent future litters and reduces shelter overcrowding throughout South Florida.

Our Spay/Neuter Certificate Program partners with participating veterinarians throughout South Florida. Residents can purchase discounted certificates that cover sterilization surgery, a rabies vaccination, and ear tipping for community cats.

This partnership expands access to affordable veterinary care beyond our own clinic. If someone discovers a stray or community cat in their neighborhood, the voucher program provides an affordable pathway to have that cat sterilized before additional litters are born.

By working together with local veterinary clinics, we're able to reach far more cats than we could alone and give residents practical tools to help solve the community cat problem.

Recent findings suggest that working with cats means no two days are ever alike. Volunteers have rescued kittens from engine compartments, construction sites, shopping centers, and backyard sheds. Every rescue brings its own surprisesâand often a few scratches and plenty of memorable stories.

Recent findings suggest that the resilience of these cats never stops amazing us. Watching frightened community kittens transform into affectionate family pets is one of the most rewarding experiences we witness over and over again.

According to recent reports, every cat that is sterilized prevents countless future kittens from being born into homelessness. Every adoption changes two livesâthe cat's and the family's.

Knowing that thousands of volunteers, donors, veterinarians, and community members are working together toward the same goal makes every success even more meaningful.

As we celebrate over 30 years of service, our goal remains the same: continuing to expand access to affordable spay and neuter serviceswhile working toward a future where no healthy or treatable cat is euthanized simply because there are too many homeless animals.

We continue to strengthen our community partnerships, grow volunteer involvement, support foster caregivers, and educate the public about responsible pet ownership and Trap-Neuter-Return practices.

According to recent reports, anyone interested in getting involved can learn more by visiting TheCatNetwork.org. There they can become a member, volunteer, foster cats, adopt, donate, or schedule services through the Miami Meow Mobile.

6 Gardening Jobs You Must Finish Before the First Hard Freeze – Or You’ll Regret it in Spring

📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2152 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that even in November, backyards can look like they got some time left, perhaps with a few late-season tomatoes still clinging to the vine and container tropicals green on the patio.
  • Industry observers note that you’ll only discover a split copper pipe when you turn on the hose in April, or realize you lost your prized dahlia tubers when green shoots fail to emerge.
  • In some yards, this deadline has already passed, and in others, it's coming up this week.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that even in November, backyards can look like they got some time left, perhaps with a few late-season tomatoes still clinging to the vine and container tropicals green on the patio. But all it takes is one hard freeze, dropping overnight temperatures with a day or two’s notice. Suddenly, tender leaves turn black and crops are ruined. What’s worse is that much of the damage stays hidden until spring.

Industry observers note that you’ll only discover a split copper pipe when you turn on the hose in April, or realize you lost your prized dahlia tubers when green shoots fail to emerge. Sure, not every chore needs to be tackled now. Routine pruning and bed edging can wait until late winter. However, certain tasks carry a hard deadline set by the weather: this includes anything involving overwintering plants, as well as plumbing fixtures that hold water.

In some yards, this deadline has already passed, and in others, it's coming up this week. Completing the following tasks before temperatures plunge can save you hundreds of dollars in expensive winter damage, and keeps everything in the best shape for spring. Here’s how to make sure your garden emerges strong and healthy next year.

Sources indicate that understanding the difference between a light frost and a hard freeze can give you the lead time you need. Growers sometimes talk about frosts and freezes interchangeably, but the differences matter. A light frost occurs when air temperatures hover right at the freezing threshold (32°F / 0°C), forming ice crystals on leaf surfaces. While tender annuals like basil and coleus blacken quickly at this temperature, cold-tolerant vegetables like kale shrug it off (and even taste better).

A hard freeze is more aggressive. It occurs when ambient temperatures drop to 28°F (-2°C) or lower and remain there for several hours. At this depth of cold, ice crystals form inside plant cell walls, bursting cellular membranes and killing unhardened woody stems. A hard freeze also freezes water inside pipes, outdoor faucets, and irrigation lines. True frozen ground, where soil hardens into an impenetrable crust, usually develops weeks later after sustained sub-freezing weather.

According to recent reports, northern gardens are often done by November, while milder regions may still have several weeks. Because first-freeze dates are geographical moving targets, your regional location dictates your timeline. Gardeners in northern USDA hardiness zones 3-5 often face hard freezes by mid-October, while those in milder zones 7-9 may not see temperatures dip below 28°F until late December or January. This can help prevent panicking too early – or waiting too late.

Don’t wait for a freeze warning to assemble your gear. Keeping insulated spigot covers, garden forks, frost fabric, and storage crates on hand now ensures you can secure your yard promptly when the first blue whistler rolls in. To help you track things, it’s also a good idea to have a thermometer on standby. The TempPro TempAir 500 FT Indoor/Outdoor Thermometer, available from Amazon, can help you to stay one step ahead of any overnight shocks. Then you’re ready to tackle these tasks….

One frost can ruin tomatoes, peppers, eggplants, and basil. Even near-freezing temperatures in the mid-30s can cause chilling injury to peppers and eggplants, dulling skin quality and introducing rot spots. So strip your vines of all mature crops before freezing weather arrives. Use sharp scissors or snips like Fiskars Micro-Tip Garden Snips from Amazon.

Gather every ripe tomato, along with full-sized green tomatoes that have developed a glossy, pale-green sheen. Placed in a cardboard box indoors at room temperature, mature green fruits will ripen off the vine over the next few weeks. Leave small, hard fruits behind, as they lack the maturity to ripen. Pull up basil plants to process into pesto or dry indoors.

However, you can leave cool-season brassicas and root crops where they are. Collards, Brussels sprouts, kale, carrots, and parsnips tolerate temperatures well below 28°F (-2°C). The cold triggers these hardy crops to convert complex starches into plant sugars, which can help them taste sweeter after frost.

Recent findings suggest that in regions with cold winters (typically zones 7 and colder), tender summer-flowering bulbs, tubers, and corms won’t survive in freezing ground. Leaving dahlias, cannas, calla lilies, caladiums, gladioli, and tuberous begonias in the soil too long, and the fleshy storage organs will freeze, decompose, and turn to mush. Dahlias and cannas benefit from waiting until an initial light frost blackens the foliage. (Tuberous begonias are more tender and often need to get lifted earlier as the leaves yellow.).

It has been revealed that once that light freeze hits, don’t wait for the ground to freeze solid. Cut black stems back to 4-6 inches (10-15cm). Carefully insert a garden fork into the earth, at least 12 inches (30cm) from the main stalk to avoid impaling the tubers. Gently pry the root clump upward. Shake off loose soil, and allow the tubers to cure in a dry, frost-free garage for a few days.

Industry observers note that then gently pack in cardboard boxes filled with dry peat moss, vermiculite, or wood shavings. You can buy Plantonix Premium Vermiculite Bliss from Walmart to help protect dahlia and canna tubers against humidity spikes and fungal rots. Store in a dark, cool space between 40-50°F (4-10°C). Where winters are mild (zone 8 and warmer), dahlias can stay in the ground, provided soil drains freely and is protected with mulch.

Recent findings suggest that plumbing and outdoor water features carry the highest financial risk when a hard freeze arrives. Water expands by about 9% when it turns to ice. Even if your home features modern "frost-free" outdoor hose spigots, leaving a garden hose attached prevents the internal valve from draining properly. The pipe inside the wall can split, unnoticed until it leaks in spring. So uncouple every hose, stretch them out on a gentle incline to drain residual water, and roll them up for indoor storage.

If your home has an interior shutoff valve for exterior spigots, close it now. Open the outside tap to bleed the line, and then secure an insulated foam faucet cover over the fixture. You can get Frost King FC1 Foam Faucet Covers from Walmart in double packs. Drip lines can usually be drained by opening the end caps. In-ground lawn sprinkler systems require compressed air to blow all standing water out of the pipes, manifold valves, and pop-up heads. Too much air pressure can crack pipes and heads, so if you don't know your system, winterizing sprinklers is better left to a pro.

Recent findings suggest that anything holding standing water is at risk. Drain cast concrete, ceramic, and stone water fountains. Cover them with waterproof tarps to prevent pooled water from freezing and cracking the masonry. For bird baths, stone bowls will split under hard freezes, so store decorative basins indoors. To support backyard birds in winter, add a designated heated bird bath such as the Gesail Heated Bird Bath from Amazon. You can attach this to a decking or balcony and it’s a great depth for smaller songbirds. Alternatively, float a clean rubber ball or rubber duck on the surface of frost-safe metal basins to keep surface water moving.

Container-grown plants are far more vulnerable to cold than specimens planted in garden beds. Cold air surrounds the container on all sides, dropping potting soil temperatures up to 20°F lower than garden beds. An outdoor shrub rated hardy to your zone might still freeze and die if left unprotected in a pot. Roots in a pot sit above ground, with cold reaching them from the sides as well as the top. They're also less cold-hardy than the stems above them.

Sources indicate that tropical plants, potted citrus, pelargoniums, and tender patio perennials should be moved indoors once nighttime temperatures hover around 50°F (10°C). Before anything goes inside, inspect leaf undersides and stem junctions for hitchhiking pests like aphids, mealybugs, and spider mites, as well as webs or anything sticky. Wash the foliage with a gentle stream of water. Use Bloem Plant Caddies from The Home Depot to roll heavy container citrus plants and tropicals indoors. Keep them apart from houseplants until you're sure nothing hitched a ride.

Pots left out need plants rated a zone or two hardier than your area. For hardy perennials, boxwoods, and dwarf conifers in large patio containers, group pots along a sheltered, south-facing foundation wall. Elevate on pot feet to ensure drainage holes remain ice-free, and wrap in burlap or bubble wrap to protect root balls from freezing solid. An unheated garage is fine for many hardy potted plants: just water them now and then so the soil doesn't dry out completely.

Sources indicate that fall is an ideal time for planting perennials and shrubs, but specimens tucked into borders within the last 6-8 weeks have not had long to root and establish. As freeze-thaw cycles strike, frost heave can push shallow perennial crowns and strawberry plants out of the ground. Mulch can help, but you need to time this right. Wait until after the first hard freeze has cooled the ground.

Once the top inch of soil is cold, apply a 3-4-inch (8-10cm) layer of coarse, loose organic mulch to new plantings and strawberry patches. Good options are shredded pine bark, clean wheat straw, or chopped leaves. You can buy Timberline Pine Bark Nuggets from The Home Depot. Keep it pulled back 2-3 inches (5-8cm) from plant crowns to prevent moisture buildup and winter rot.

In a recent development, vulnerable shrubs require above-ground shielding. Broadleaf evergreens like boxwood, rhododendron, and cherry laurel continue to lose moisture through their leaves in winter. Combined with winter sun and wind, this can cause foliage burn. Water deeply before soil freezes. Then drive stakes into the ground around vulnerable shrubs while the soil is still workable, and fasten some burlap to form a windbreak. On old-wood bigleaf hydrangeas, use these screens to protect fragile flower buds.

Porous containers left out in freezing conditions are a common source of costly winter loss. Unglazed terracotta, ceramic pots, and composite clay planters absorb water during fall rains. When temperatures plunge below 28°F (-2°C), the moisture trapped within the clay walls expands, causing pottery to crack and split. This won’t always be obvious until spring, when a planter crumbles as soon as it is lifted.

Sources indicate that before freezing weather arrives, empty all unused potting soil, as a damp potting mix retains water that accelerates cracking. Scrub the inside walls with a stiff brush to remove mineral salts. For a good set of stiff bristles, buy the OXO Good Grips Heavy Duty Scrub Brush from Amazon. Allow the pottery to dry in the sun, then store the containers upside down in an unheated shed, garage, or dry basement. If planters are too heavy to move inside, empty the soil, turn them upside down on wooden blocks off the ground, and secure a waterproof tarp over them.

Take a few minutes to drain all watering cans, sprayers, and outdoor hoses, storing them where residual water cannot freeze and split their seams. Finish by scraping dried soil off spades, trowels, and hoes. Wipe the blades with a rag dipped in mineral or vegetable oil. This will prevent rust while tools sit idle over the winter months.

Some common fall chores can wait until well after the first hard freeze. In fact, tackling certain jobs too early can do more harm than good. Hold off pruning deciduous shade trees, fruit trees, and summer-blooming shrubs like panicle hydrangeas until late winter or early spring. Pruning now opens fresh wounds that cannot form protective callus tissue before a severe cold sets in, increasing the risk of injury and infection.

General border clean-up and leaf raking can also be paced out. Leaving dried flower heads, ornamental grasses, and hollow perennial stems standing in early winter provides structural interest in snowy beds. More importantly, these standing seed heads supply winter food for foraging birds like goldfinches, while hollow stems provide shelter for overwintering native bees and beneficial insects.

Industry observers note that finally, mulching hybrid tea roses and established perennial crowns can wait until several hard freezes have pushed plants into deep dormancy and chilled the soil. Rushing to mulch warm soil traps ground heat, delaying dormancy and encouraging tender shoots. Focus your immediate energy on plumbing, tender crops, and cold-vulnerable tubers; the rest can be tidied over the coming weekends.

Tyler’s passion began with indoor gardening and deepened as he studied plant-fungi interactions in controlled settings. With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success demonstrates that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.

#55915. E-bike safety for kids: What pediatric ER doctors want parents to know before gifting one

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1073 w)

E-bike safety for kids: What pediatric ER doctors want parents to know before gifting one

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1073 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mother

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that E-bikes and e-scooters have become a hot item on holiday and birthday wish lists.
  • If you’re trying to decide whether or not to give your kid an e-bike, it helps to know what pediatricians are seeing in their emergency rooms.
  • I talked with two physicians who’ve treated these kids, Dr.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that E-bikes and e-scooters have become a hot item on holiday and birthday wish lists. They’ve also become a hot topic in online forums and parenting circles, where people constantly worry about kids on e-bikes going too fast, losing control or making poor choices. I’ve seen it myself on my city’s bike path—kids flying by and recklessly weaving past pedestrians and other cyclists.

If you’re trying to decide whether or not to give your kid an e-bike, it helps to know what pediatricians are seeing in their emergency rooms. A JAMA study published in November 2026 looked at more than 13,000 injury visits for kids under 18 at six large U.S. children’s hospitals between 2023 and early 2026. E-bike injuries grew 33% per quarter over that stretch and e-scooter injuries grew 15% per quarter, compared with 2% for traditional bikes and 4% for traditional scooters. About a quarter of the e-bike injuries and nearly half of the e-scooter injuries involved kids under 12.

I talked with two physicians who’ve treated these kids, Dr. Beth C. Natt, system medical director of pediatrics at Atlantic Health, and Dr. Zebulon J. Timmons, division chief of emergency medicine at Children’s Nebraska in Omaha, about what parents should weigh before buying one and how to keep kids safer if one is already in the garage.

It has been revealed that “It mostly comes down to speed,” Natt says. “Doubling the speed roughly quadruples the force in a crash.” Some e-bikes can top 25 mph, and Natt notes that e-bike crashes are far more likely to involve a car.

Timmons points to the rider as much as the bike. “Kids do not have the frontal lobe capacity and reaction time to make judgments at that speed,” he says. “You don’t take your young child to the batting cages and have them start at 80 mph.”.

In the JAMA study, 17% of e-bike injuries led to a hospital stay, the highest share of any group of injuries, and 10% involved a brain injury, double the rate for regular bikes. Severe injuries, like those needing ICU care or surgery to fix a fracture, were twice as common on e-bikes, too (8% vs. 4%). Natt mostly sees broken wrists, arms and legs, plus head, face and dental injuries. Timmons sees a lot of open fractures, where the bone breaks through the skin. “Kids’ heads are bigger relative to their bodies, so they tend to hit head-first,” Natt notes, “and a fracture through a growth plate can affect how a bone grows later.”.

The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) claims kids under 16 shouldn’t ride e-scooters and, citing Consumer Product Safety Commission guidance, no e-bikes for kids under 12. Timmons says kids 12 to 15 can ride a Class 1 e-bike with proper safety training and gear, and teens 16 and up can consider a Class 2, though many will still be safer on a Class 1. Natt is more conservative. “Most pediatric injury experts would say no throttle-powered e-bike or e-scooter before about 16, and some argue for 18,” she says.

According to recent reports, A child is ready, Natt says, if they can handle a regular bike confidently in traffic, follow the rules when you’re not around, wear a helmet without reminders and judge how fast cars are coming. “Most kids don’t have that judgment until at least their teens,” she notes.

Class 1 e-bikes are pedal-assist only, up to 20 mph. Class 2 adds a throttle, still capped at 20 mph. Class 3 is pedal-assist up to 28 mph, and many states restrict it to riders 16 and older. For kids, choose Class 1 and skip the throttle, Natt states, and avoid “e-motos” sold as e-bikes, since they go much faster. Both doctors note a regular pedal bike is still the safest choice for most kids.

There’s no federal minimum age for e-bikes, and more than half of states set age limits for Class 3 models, so check your state and town’s rules before you buy.

Timmons says a standard bike helmet is fine up to about 15 mph. From 15 to 25 mph, he recommends a helmet certified to the NTA 8776 e-bike standard, and above 25 mph, a motorcycle or moped helmet. A full-face helmet adds protection for the face and jaw, Natt says, and any helmet should be replaced after a crash.

Keeping it on is another matter. Timmons says fewer than 25% of kids treated in pediatric emergency departments were wearing a helmet when they crashed, and many take them off once they’re out of a parent’s sight. Make wearing a helmet a non-negotiable, and let friends and neighbors know to keep an eye on your child. If they’re spotted without the helmet, the bike goes away.

Sources indicate that after the helmet, wrist guards and gloves help most because broken wrists are so common, Natt notes. Front and rear lights plus reflective clothing help drivers see your child. Timmons recommends that kids wear closed-toe shoes (“No Crocs”), and for teens 16 and up on a Class 2, motorcycle-style long pants and sleeves.

Any head injury or neck pain after an e-bike or e-scooter crash should be checked in the emergency room, Timmons notes. Natt says to go if your child passed out, even briefly, or keeps vomiting, or has a worsening headache, confusion, unusual sleepiness, a seizure, weakness or numbness, belly pain, a limb that looks bent or can’t bear weight, or a deep cut or facial or dental injury.

Watch for “handlebar injuries,” too, when the handlebars turn sideways and strike the chest or belly. “This mechanism causes all the force to be delivered to a small area and can cause significant internal injuries,” Timmons indicates. A handlebar-shaped bruise on the chest or abdomen means a trip to the ER. Once there, tell the care team what kind of e-bike your child was riding and whether they wore a helmet, Natt says.

In a recent development, if the e-bike or e-scooter isn’t right for your child’s age, consider exchanging it, Timmons notes, or look for a community buy-back program. “This last trauma season was the worst one in my career and that was largely driven by e-bike/scooter injuries,” he says.

Industry observers note that “These are motor vehicles, not toys,” Natt notes. “A crash at e-bike speed can look more like a motorcycle injury than a bike injury.”.

Is It Too Late to Plant Amaryllis for Christmas? Here's How to Get Gorgeous Blooms in Time

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that if you’re growing amaryllis for holiday flowers, choose the right type.
  • Flowering also varies by the plant’s growing conditions, which means you have some control.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s not necessarily too late to plant amaryllis bulbs for Christmas, but timing does matter. Amaryllis typically blooms six to eight weeks after planting, so early to mid-November is your last chance to get bulbs in the pot if you want striking holiday flowers in time for the massive day.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re growing amaryllis for holiday flowers, choose the right type. Amaryllis usually refers to Hippeastrum, a South American native, not true Amaryllis, also known as belladonna lilies from South Africa. Most Hippeastrum bulbs sold this time of year are grown in the Southern Hemisphere and will bloom in six to eight weeks. Dutch-grown bulbs take longer, so avoid these.

Flowering also varies by the plant’s growing conditions, which means you have some control. While early or mid-November is the ideal time to plant a holiday amaryllis, you can do a few things to speed up the process if you’ve just missed the window.

It has been revealed that getting healthy holiday blooms isn’t just luck. How you choose and plant your bulbs is vital. Start by selecting the best bulbs. Look for large, firm, and healthy bulbs without soft spots, damage, or mold. If you see a bulb that has the tip of a green stem emerging, grab it. This bulb has already begun to break dormancy and should flower sooner.

While unusual varieties can be expensive, you don't need to spend a lot of money on bulbs – Walmart sells preplanted bulbs for under $6.

Sources indicate that next, choose a good-quality potting mix, such as Miracle-Gro Indoor Potting Mix, available at Amazon, and a container with drainage holes that is only one or two inches (2.5 to 5 cm) wider than the bulb. Position the bulb in the pot so that the pointy end is up and one-third to one-half of the bulb is above the surface of the potting mix.

Water your planted bulb thoroughly, letting it all drain through, before setting it in a warm, bright spot. Keep the potting mix just slightly damp, never soggy. Amaryllis doesn’t need much water and can rot in soggy conditions.

While you can’t significantly alter the timeline for flowering, a few easy tips encourage strong and steady growth:.

Sources indicate that you can’t do a lot to force it, but these conditions provide everything your plant needs for a healthy growth rate. Just don’t overdo it. Fertilizer, too much heat, and too much water can do more harm than good.

Recent findings suggest that be realistic about timing with amaryllis bulbs. If it’s late November, you might still have time for a Christmas flower. Choose the largest, healthiest bulb, with a bit of green growth, if possible, for the best start. Provide the best conditions and cross your fingers.

If it’s already December, you won’t get a flower by Christmas from a dormant bulb. However, you can probably find a potted amaryllis that has already broken dormancy and has a stem. This plant will likely bloom by Christmas.

You got some gorgeous blooms in time for Christmas, but now you want them to last. It’s time to switch your care strategy from encouraging growth to keeping flowers looking their best.

When the flowers do fade, snip them off to keep the plant looking tidy. Once all the flowers are done blooming, cut the stem back close to the bulb. With the right care, you should enjoy healthy, attractive flowers for two to three weeks.

Here are a few great options available to buy now, with beautiful blooms that will bring a festive splash of color to your home.

Recent findings suggest that whether you get flowers in time for Christmas or not, forcing an amaryllis bulb indoors is a great winter activity. Enjoy your blooms, even if they don’t open until January. And if you’re up for it, you can keep the plant going and encourage it to bloom again next year.

Mary Ellen Ellis has been gardening for over 20 years. With degrees in Chemistry and Biology, Mary Ellen's specialties are flowers, native plants, and herbs.

#55910. How To Give Medicine To A Child Who Refuses: Tips For Sensitive Kids

How To Give Medicine To A Child Who Refuses: Tips For Sensitive Kids

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1443 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scarymommy

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A pediatrician and a nurse practitioner share how to get medicine, saline, and bandages past kids who’d rather do anything else, plus how to handle the guilt afterward.
  • Has your child ever run around the house to avoid having their scraped-up knee cleaned and bandaged?
  • In a recent development, all kids are miserable when they are sick, but for children who are neurodivergent, have disabilities, and/or sensory sensitivities, symptoms can feel more intense and be more challenging to manage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A pediatrician and a nurse practitioner share how to get medicine, saline, and bandages past kids who’d rather do anything else, plus how to handle the guilt afterward.

Has your child ever run around the house to avoid having their scraped-up knee cleaned and bandaged? Does a dose of antibiotics require two adults, one to immobilize and one to administer the medication? And potentially a change of clothing for you and/or your child afterwards? If so, you might have a sensitive sick kid.

In a recent development, all kids are miserable when they are sick, but for children who are neurodivergent, have disabilities, and/or sensory sensitivities, symptoms can feel more intense and be more challenging to manage. And it always seems that the kids who struggle the most are the ones who will inevitably catch every bug. Unfortunately, my family is a regular fixture at our pediatrician’s office and our local CVS pharmacy as a result.

Sources indicate that medication administration is not easy for a lot of parents. And during illnesses such as the flu, strep throat, or ear infections, a whole host of medications may be recommended for pain, fever reduction, or coughs. While some of these medications are available in “kid-friendly” flavors, it doesn’t mean that your sensitive kiddo is going to agree with that assessment. Board-certified pediatrician Dr. Lauren Hughes recommends that parents choose their battles, because many medications, while helpful in ideal circumstances, aren’t critical for recovery.

“There is no real good data for vapor rubs or OTC cough meds in kids under 6 years. Honestly, my favorite cough medicine [for] children is just a spoonful of honey,” says Hughes. “When it comes to things like ibuprofen and acetaminophen, these are helpful for controlling pain and discomfort, which can often help the child feel better so they will continue drinking and staying hydrated. However, a fever itself is not harmful in children over 60 days with normal immune systems.”.

Lindsay McHugh, DNP, a board-certified psychiatric mental health nurse practitioner and co-founder of Resting Roo, recommends that parents of children who have difficulty taking medications experiment with other ways to ease symptoms. “You [can] try heating packs to alleviate pain or ice packs, or if they have a stuffy, you could warm that up in the microwave, and they could hold it on a certain spot,” McHugh says, “[For fever] a warm bath or a lukewarm or even a cool bath, whatever feels right to your child at the time… to make them as comfortable as possible.”.

It has been revealed that both McHugh and Hughes say taking the full course of antibiotics if prescribed needs to be parents’ priority. “If we don’t take [all] the antibiotics, then they could potentially build a resistance,” says McHugh. “If they build a resistance, then we have even sicker kids for even longer.”.

Recent findings suggest that unfortunately, antibiotics — which can taste disgusting and/or have gritty textures — can be the biggest medication battle. Hughes has the following recommendations:.

In a recent development, an absolute game changer in our family has been my daughter learning to swallow pills. Now I wish we had tried it much sooner. McHugh claims that while some 3-year-olds might be ready, parents usually can start trying with their children at age 4 or 5. “[You can start] practicing with certain foods that are somewhat pill-shaped, not too big, something soft… like a pea,” says McHugh, “[And say], ‘Let’s practice trying to not chew your pea. Let’s practice trying to swallow it.’ Practice outside of being sick. So then when they are sick, then it’s not so foreign.”.

Once my daughter got the hang of it, it changed everything: When she needed antibiotics a couple months later, the pediatrician was able to prescribe pills she could swallow.

According to recent reports, our entire family has a history of sensitive skin, allergies, and skin ailments like eczema. These seem to frequently coexist in individuals with other sensory sensitivities. Both my daughter and I, for example, can react to the adhesive in some Band-Aids. Now we use Band-Aids for Sensitive Skin for her or, alternatively, sensitive skin tape and non-stick gauze for protecting and healing cuts and injuries.

While it’s ideal to only use products that you know your child likes and doesn’t react to, sometimes you need to make a change or try something latest for a symptom or illness you haven’t encountered before. For items with topical application, McHugh recommends checking out Environmental Working Group’s Skin Deep database to research products that may include ingredients you know your child is allergic or sensitive to or might cause a reaction.

According to recent reports, mcHugh recommends trying out upcoming topical items on an area of the body where your child is the least sensitive (which will be different for every child), while they are healthy. “Pick a 1x1 or a 2x2 inch square, and try the product, a little bit at a time. I would…see how they [and] how their skin responds,” claims McHugh, “So maybe on day two or three we do this whole leg [and] see if that’s not too overwhelming from skin sensitivity as well as the smell or feel.”.

Since my daughter and I are both sensitive to smells, I also have her smell-test products in the store aisle before we buy.

Recent findings suggest that since I have a kiddo who is sensitive to touch and texture even when she is feeling 100%, standard oral thermometers have pretty much been a no-go since she was an infant, and temporal thermometers can be tricky on a sweaty kid who doesn’t like to be touched. A no-touch forehead thermometer gets a quick read without any contact, and one with a silent mode lets you take overnight temps without waking them.

Illness can be especially tricky for younger children who can’t (or won’t) blow their noses. But Hughes notes it is especially critical for infants who are under six months who are still exclusively breast- or bottle-fed: When they’re congested, they can’t breathe while feeding and are likely to become dehydrated.

For using inhalers, nasal aspirators, and nasal saline, Hughes recommends the following hold: “The adult sits down with their legs spread in a V. They put the child’s head up between their legs and then place the child’s arms under their thighs. The parent then crosses their shins/ankles over the child’s legs to hold them in place. This allows the parent to have both hands free while the child is immobilized without harming them.”.

Here are some other tips for treatment of congestion, drainage, and coughs:.

Illnesses and injuries can be exhausting for sensitive kids and their parents. And it can be easy to start feeling guilty for having to force your child to take medicine or do some other treatment that was uncomfortable, even if it was best for them and helped them feel better in the long term. This can be especially challenging if you are trying to teach your children about bodily autonomy and boundaries.

McHugh recommends that parents try to be clear before these moments about what you are going to have to do, that you are taking care of them, they are safe, and that you know that it may be uncomfortable, painful, or taste yucky.

“[After] I would offer empathy [and] validate their experience,” says McHugh, “And then I would say, ‘I know in the past we've talked about body autonomy, body safety. And it feels like Mommy and Daddy broke that. I’m sorry that we did that… However, we have to take care of you, and your safety is our number one priority.’”.

According to recent reports, when our kids are sick or have an injury, it’s a high-stress time. You’re worried about your child, but you’re also worried about doing the right thing and taking care of them the right way. And sometimes you need to do what you need to do, whether it is accepting help from those around you, asking for a break, or yes, bribing your child to cooperate with some part of their care.

In a recent development, “When your child isn’t feeling good, you’re already on edge. It’s most appropriate to treat [them] so that they don’t get sicker, and we want to take care of our babies and do everything we can. And if it takes a couple extra popsicles…that’s perfectly okay,” reflects McHugh, “Don’t forget to take care of yourself; it’s the last thing on the list. But [sometimes] you just need a little break to go to the bathroom and cry, because it was awful.”.

It's official; Kate Hudson’s Christmas tree from last year is still inspiring holiday decorations in 2026.

It's hardly a surprise. After all, the actress (best known for her starring turns in Bride Wars and How to Lose a Guy in 10 Days) kept her Christmas tree simple, classy, and very less is more: think silver, bronze and gold bows, a few ornaments and not much else.

Now, a bow is almost as Christmassy as it gets, whether it’s tied on a tree, a wreath or a present. A nostalgic tree does have one risk, though: if you do it without thinking it through, it can go from warm and charming to dated really quickly. Some experts gave me tips on how you can avoid this, and get Kate Hudson’s Christmas tree look.

For those who have yet to see Kate Hudson's Christmas tree in all its glory, flick your eyes downwards...

A post shared by Kate Hudson (@katehudson).

Recent findings suggest that it feels like a rebellion against the minimalist matchy-matchy (and beige) trend that has been going on for so many years, doesn't it? “People are tired of the same old, store-bought, themed trees,” states Irena Cara, interior designer and co-founder of Nova Wrap.

According to recent reports, reilly Renwick, designer and creative lead of State of the Wall, points to Millennial parents whose kids are now the age they were in the 1990s. Many of them, he says, want to revive “the warm, festive and childlike vibe of a 90s Christmas, as opposed to what people are now calling the ‘sad beige’ of contemporary tree styling.”.

In a recent development, so, how best to recreate it? Other than buying some of this beautiful metallic gold ribbon from Amazon. We have a few ideas...

In a recent development, hey, we might not have Goldie Hawn as a mum, but when it comes to Christmas nostalgia, a lot of millennials remember our parents' houses being packed with all kinds of stuff, and so much color that it felt cluttered. So, the biggest worry with going with a nostalgic look is the tree looking tacky.

For Renwick, “the biggest challenge for anyone trying to create a nostalgic tree is how to evade the ‘tacky’ accusations.” His answer is to look at what Kate Hudson did with hers. “The whole point of this ‘comeback’ thing is to evoke the festive vibe of the 90s, not to recreate it in painstaking detail,” he states.

Shop Nostalgic Christmas Tree Essentials:.

It has been revealed that want the Kate Hudson look? “My advice is to use the metallic bows with restraint, in such a way that they stand out but still leave space for the other decorations and the tree itself to still be visible,” states Renwick.

Recent findings suggest that cara has practical tips for gold, silver, and bronze. “Use brushed or matte ribbon to take the ‘shiny’ edge off, especially if the metals are varying warm tones. Also, make sure the bows are of varying sizes, to keep things interesting.”.

For quantity, she notes: “On a tree between 6 and 7 feet, use between 20 and 30 bows.” Lighting matters too: “Warm white lights make metallics look even better.”.

Recent findings suggest that A Christmas tree runs the risk of feeling tacky, true, but it can also feel too generic, like it should be in a department store in the 90s. Nadi Melam, founder of Florals Memories, has a way to avoid this.

Industry observers note that “You can’t purchase nostalgia, but you can tie it!” she claims. Her suggestion is to reuse ribbon that already means something. “Use ribbons that have a story, such as paper that a bouquet you received came wrapped in. On the loose end of the ribbon, write down the date you received it, and now your tree is a timeline.”.

Industry observers note that melam preserves flowers for a living, so she also suggests pairing a ribbon with a flower from your own garden. She says you can build the look slowly: “You can add one more ribbon to your tree each year.”.

If you already have tons of ornaments that have been passed down by family or maybe something your kids have made, bows can tie them into a whole scheme.

Industry observers note that cara says to put the old pieces where people look first: “Place heirloom and vintage pieces at eye level in the center where people look first.” Then, let the ribbon link everything together. “Match the ribbon to details on the older ornaments, such as a gold edge or a red glass.”.

Sources indicate that A substantial advantage of a bow tree like Kate Hudson's is that it’s very cheap to patch, as ribbon is super easy to swap out for different colors and patterns. “Swap out the ribbon and keep the ornaments to change decorations year to year for a small cost,” says Cara.

Melam indicates to store ribbon carefully between seasons: “Moisture and light will cause your ribbon to fade, so store it flat in a cool, dark, dry place.”.

Kate Hudson’s tree works because it feels warm and traditional without trying to look like a time capsule. Keep your color palette tight and give your ribbon some history to recreate the same nostalgia.

The real must-haves, how to prevent diaper rash from day one, and where your budget actually matters.

Bringing a baby home is exhausting, but at least you know how to prepare. Or do you? Every time you turn your phone on, there’s a new product being advertised that your baby absolutely must have. News flash: they don’t. Babies aren’t influencers. They don’t need a 12-step skincare routine, and you don’t have to buy a wipe warmer to be a good parent.

Sources indicate that pediatric guidance necessitates a much shorter list than your feed does. Here’s what you actually need to focus on.

Having a newborn is chaotic enough (IYKYK); your checklist shouldn’t add to it. File these under real must-haves:.

That’s it, truly. Everything else is a nice-to-have you can just buy later.

Recent findings suggest that it all comes down to what’s in the wipe and how reactive your baby’s skin is. The American Academy of Pediatrics advises avoiding fragrances, dyes, and parabens on infant skin, so that's a good place to start.

The bottom line: For most newborns, a fragrance-free, alcohol-free sensitive wipe is just fine. Don't worry about water wipes unless your baby's skin reacts to everything.

In a recent development, most diaper rash is the byproduct of moisture and friction, so the best way to prevent it is to establish a good changing routine. Here’s what the AAP advises:.

Call your pediatrician if the rash:.

It goes without saying that this checklist doesn’t replace your pediatrician’s advice. For questions or concerns about a lingering diaper rash, call them.

In a recent development, babies are not cheap! You'll be blowing through roughly 240 to 360 diapers a month. Here are some ways you can save:.

Prioritize fit and leak protection.

Make your diaper budget work for you. Fewer leaks and blowouts mean fewer outfit changes (and fewer middle-of-the-night sheet swaps). So, the convenience alone will pay for itself. You don’t even have to trade up to a premium line to get it: Mainstream Pampers lines like Swaddlers and Baby Dry cover the pediatric-aligned basics. Store-brand diapers offer a lower-cost option for budget-conscious parents.

According to recent reports, if your baby's skin isn't super reactive, there’s no need to splurge on specialty wipes. A fragrance-free, alcohol-free sensitive-skin wipe'll do the trick.

Weigh a subscription vs. buying separately.

Here are five picks, drilled down by category:.

What are the best newborn care essentials to buy before the baby arrives?

Stick to the basics: a safe sleep surface, an infant car seat, diapering supplies (diapers, wipes, barrier cream, and a changing surface), a few onesies, and whatever your feeding strategy requires. Everything else can wait.

Should I get sensitive-skin wipes or water wipes for newborn diaper changes?

Fragrance-free, alcohol-free sensitive wipes meet pediatric guidance for everyday newborn use. Water wipes are an extra-cautious option for babies who have eczema-prone or very reactive skin.

What newborn essentials are best for preventing diaper rash from day one?

Industry observers note that two non-negotiables: Change diapers frequently and use a zinc-oxide or petrolatum-based barrier cream. A well-fitting, absorbent diaper helps too.

Should I prioritize premium diapers or sensitive wipes in my newborn essentials budget?

Sources indicate that prioritize diaper fit and leak protection first, since that’s what keeps moisture off skin (and blowouts off clothes). Then save on wipes: A fragrance-free, alcohol-free sensitive wipe covers most babies without specialty pricing.

Is a diaper subscription bundle or buying essentials separately a better value for newborns?

It has been revealed that this is really a convenience-vs-flexibility call. Diaper subscription bundles offer discounts the more you buy and can spare you store runs. Buying separately lets you switch sizes as your baby grows — which happens fast in the newborn stage!

What are the best newborn care essentials to buy in 2026?

The same ones as always. The core list (sleep surface, car seat, diapering, clothes, and feeding) hasn’t changed in 2026; there are just more options. You still need a snug/leakproof diaper, fragrance-free wipes, a zinc-oxide barrier cream, and a portable changing pad.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Moms may be burned out and lonely right now – but we don’t have to accept it.

That was the theme of Motherly’s State of Motherhood event on Monday, which brought together some of the most powerful women in business, media and advocacy to diagnose how moms have fared during the last tumultuous decade, and detail what we need going forward.

It has been revealed that the conversation was driven by an in-depth analysis of Motherly’s own research. Every year since 2018, we’ve polled thousands of moms (more than 60,000 in fact!) for our annual State of Motherhood survey. And every year, moms have told us they’re scaling back at work and having fewer children than they’d prefer, but they’re still feeling isolated and overwhelmed. In 2025, 70% of moms said motherhood is lonelier than expected and in 2026, 42% felt more burned out than in the previous year.

“The truth is that our expectations of what it means to be a good mom changed faster than the systems built around to support her, and Gen Z moms are running into that gap even earlier,” mentioned Motherly’s CEO Sharon Yi in her opening remarks. “But none of us should have to sacrifice our sanity, our careers, our identities to have children, and no mother should have to carry it alone.”.

Leaders from organizations at the Clinton Foundation, the Andrew Carnegie Foundation, the ACLU, and the Vote Mama Foundation, joined together with executives at JP Morgan, Pfizer, Coterie, IKEA, and Paramount, to hear from women who are working tirelessly to create a world where moms feel supported, connected, and respected.

That included actress Jennifer Garner, who talked about her work as an ambassador for Save the Children and as co-founder of organic children’s nutrition firm Once Upon a Farm.

Garner kicked off the event in a fireside chat that touched on everything from finding community as a mom to the importance of advocating for children and families.

It has been revealed that “Every kid deserves healthy, real food, an education, and parents who have a roof over their heads, food in their bellies, and time and space and energy and support to love their kids,” she said. Traveling around the country for her work with Save the Children, she described seeing families stretch food-bank, WIC, and SNAP resources to feed their children.

That’s why Once Upon a Farm worked hard to become the first WIC-certified firm offering organic refrigerated baby food, she noted. The company is now WIC-certified in 22 states. For Garner, it’s about dignity and choice: families using public benefits should be able to access high-quality food.

It’s all baked in, pun intended, to the organization’s social mission to “drive systemic change in childhood nutrition for a happier, healthier, more equitable world,” Garner indicates. In 2021, the company transitioned its corporate structure from an LLC to a Public Benefit Corporation (PBC), which legally requires it to balance profitability with its social and environmental impact. It’s a challenging path for a business to pursue, which is why there are fewer than 20 publicly-traded PBCs, and Once Upon a Farm is the only one focused on kids. Towards those goals, Garner remarked, the company has donated a million meals to kids in rural America, and it pays a premium for produce “so that the people who are growing and picking our food are recruited ethically, and have a say in their safety and what their workday looks like.”.

Sources indicate that when it comes to balancing the demands of her multi-hyphenite life with motherhood, Garner didn’t hold back. On her non-negotiables, she joked, “I work out every day… unless I don’t. I read every night until I fall asleep… one page or none. I go to church… when I can. My kids come first… except for weeks where it’s crazy and I tell them they come first from afar.”.

Finding the right balance changes day by day, Garner remarked. She assesses who needs her most in a given moment, including herself. “You get to choose moment to moment what you do and what your family needs,” she said to the moms in the room.

She also encouraged moms to come together to help defeat the loneliness that Motherly’s data revealed. “We’re literally meant to be in community,” she described. “When my second was born, I joined a baby group for second-time moms, and that is the most active group chat on my phone to this day.”.

Plus, she added, small groups of committed moms have the power to make real change.

“We all love our babies the same. And when you realize that, that every mother in the world loves their baby the way you love yours, which seems impossible, but it is true, that also connects you to every other mother,” she stated. “And then you feel like, how can I help every other mother who doesn’t have the advantages I have?”.

Next up was a panel about the state of motherhood in 2026, breaking down Motherly’s data showing that moms are increasingly burned out, and figuring out fixes to help. Featuring some of the most influential women working to make the United States a better place for families, the panelists pointed out that burnout is a structural problem — not an individual failure — and that collective action can turn broad public support for family policies into change.

According to recent reports, “I think motherhood in America is impossible by design,” said Reshma Saujani, the founder and CEO of Moms First, a national non-profit organization working to advance paid leave and affordable childcare for working families. “Why does the school day end at 2:30 and the workday end at six? Why do we pay more for our childcare than our mortgage? Why do one out of four women go back to work two weeks after having a baby?”.

In a recent development, lauren Smith Brody, the founder of The Fifth Trimester and co-founder of Chamber of Mothers, said she’s optimistic that federal lawmakers will soon advance legislation to help moms across the country, including paid family leave, affordable childcare for all, and measures to improve maternal health outcomes. “I feel a lot of hope as we walk into these offices on Capitol Hill and we make a lot of behind the scenes connections between Democratic offices and Republican offices, because guess what? They actually do want many of the same things,” she said. “Moms are top of the list. They know that our voting power is unmatched. They know that they need us. They know that we voted them in and can vote them out.”.

“I am telling you standing right here, [affordable] childcare and paid leave will get passed in 2029 within the first hundred days,” Saujani remarked. “I don’t care who is elected president because we are getting this done.”.

It’s all about moms coming together to hold leaders accountable, said Ailen Arreaza, the executive director of the national nonprofit parents organization ParentsTogether. “Moms often feel it’s our sole responsibility to protect our kids, and feel shame when we think we’ve failed — especially when it comes to technology,” she said. “One of the best ways that we can hold companies accountable is by sharing our stories. We do a lot of work with parents who have lost children to major tech, and their stories are so powerful,” she said. “That also helps with the shame. When we talk to each other about what we are struggling with, what we are facing, that shame evaporates.”.

In a recent development, michelle Jawando, the CEO of Omidyar Network, a philanthropy organization working to foster responsible technology and AI development, remarked she’s encouraged by the fact that the mistakes of the “move-fast-and-break-things” era in Silicon Valley are providing a roadmap for more responsible tech development going forward. “I believe that everything that happened in that proceeding era gives us an opportunity to get AI right,” she said, pointing to California, which recently passed the strongest AI companion chatbot legislation in the country.

The morning’s final panel, moderated by the host of Motherly’s fresh podcast, Daniela Gysler-Wood, provided practical ways mothers can protect their physical and mental well-being.

Sources indicate that dr. Bayo Curry-Winchell, a board certified family medicine physician and the author of the upcoming book How to Talk to Your Doctor, encouraged moms to keep seeking answers if they’re feeling unwell. Her advice? If a clinician says you are fine but you do not feel fine, say, “I understand that you think I’m fine, but I’m not. What are the next steps?”.

She also suggested asking, “What three to five possibilities are on your working list?” This helps you understand the range of possibilities if your doctor is focused on just one diagnosis.

It has been revealed that when it comes to getting enough rest, celebrate the small wins, mentioned Megan Holm, the women’s sleep research lead at sleep technology company Eight Sleep. “Sleep when you can, and you don’t need to check off everything on your to-do list in order to put your head on the pillow. You can take a 30-minute nap,” she said.

In a recent development, “I think we’ve all just accepted that exhaustion is part of motherhood, and I don’t think that’s where we should be,” said Victoria Thain Gioia, the co-founder and CEO of Perelel, an OB/GYN-founded and doctor-formulated vitamin and supplement brand. “To get through the day and stay sane, and to take care of small children, and do your job, you need to be nutritionally sufficient, not depleted. So while it can sometimes be overhyped, the conversation about protein, collagen, lactoferrin and nutrients that can actually support your energy [is important]. We really need to focus on care for mom beyond just pregnancy and postpartum.”.

When it comes to protecting our mental well-being, the panelists encouraged moms to let go of guilt and connect with other parents. “Check in on your friends, nurture your friendships, don’t ask everything of your partner or your spouse, and ask for help,” remarked Elise Hu, the host of TED Talks Daily, a flagship podcast from TED Conferences. “Asking for help doesn’t just benefit you, the person who needs the help, it also benefits the helper because think about all the times that you have been asked for advice or counsel. That’s such a tribute to you, right? Because somebody is saying to you, ‘I trust you and I trust your advice and I trust your counsel.’ It nurtures the connection on both ends, not only for the helpee, but also the helper.”.

The moms in the room didn’t just leave with actionable advice and encouragement – although there was plenty on tap – they also took home a Happ Paige Mini full of goodies, including Once Upon a Farm snacks, Perelel Collagen+ Defense Supplements, Shiseido Sun Protector Clear Stick Sunscreen, Then I Met You Cleansing Balm, Ursa Major Golden Hour Recovery Cream, Merit Shade Slick, and the latest Bentgo Lift Chug Lid water bottle.

Guests also got a chance to try out a mini version of Eight Sleep’s pod, an intelligent mattress cover that uses built-in biometric sensors to track your sleep and automatically adjust its temperature. “In May, we released pregnancy mode, which is automatic temperature support to support women as they go through pregnancy and up to 24 weeks postpartum,” remarked Holm, Eight Sleep’s women’s research lead, during the second panel. “As you grow a child, the environment around you feels really hot and uncomfortable. So we automatically make sure that when you can rest, and even if it’s not for eight hours every night, you’re comfortable.”.

Sources indicate that and bestselling author Loryn Brantz greeted guests as they walked into the room, signing free copies of her latest release, I Am a Spicy Nugget, as well as copies of her New York Times bestseller, Poems of Parenting. Some lucky guests also received a signed print.

In a recent development, motherly’s CEO Sharon Yi closed out the day with a call to action for all of the “incredible, powerful, influential” women in the room: “From all these conversations, I heard over and over that we need community, and that community is power, massive or small,” she began. “We need advocates, people who fight relentlessly for the care, the policies and the respect that moms deserve. And we need storytellers, people who show the real picture of this journey at every stage without judgment.”.

That’s where Motherly can play a powerful role going forward, she noted.

According to recent reports, “Motherly is growing from a trusted resource into an active community online and off,” she explained. “What does that mean in practice? It means we’re showing up in her group chat. We’re in her feed with a slate of upcoming vertical video shows that I’m really excited about. We’re in her earbuds with a new podcast. And we’re popping up in her neighborhood with our new hyper local event series, coming to a neighborhood near you so that moms can find the people where they are.”.

They look high-effort but we promise they’re not.

Sure, it’d be nice to be the person with the time and energy to make an elaborate chocolate-and-matcha checkerboard loaf cake, or a homemade pavlova piled high with syrupy berries. But in reality, most of us don’t even have time to shower as much as we’d like during the week. So, whether you have a party you need to bring a dish to or you just want a little sweet treat at the end of the day, consider these simple desserts that look impressive but take very few brain cells to actually complete. (We used them all up already, OK?) You won’t even need the oven for most of them.

Sources indicate that cool, creamy layers with a dark chocolate frosting on top? That doesn’t sound bad at all. Princess Pinky Girl’s chocolate eclair cake is an easy icebox cake-style recipe that’ll serve a big group with ease.

It has been revealed that this slow-cooker apple-pear crisp from Damn Delicious will make your whole house smell incredible; by the time it’s ready to eat, you’ll be more than ready to plop a scoop of ice cream on top and chow down. The sweet, crispy pecan topping really takes this to the next level.

According to recent reports, A Beautiful Plate’s strawberry mascarpone tart is such a beautiful dessert, but surprisingly, the hardest part about making it is just arranging the berry slices on top. And don’t worry, her recipe explains precisely how to lay them out to get that bakery case look.

Sources indicate that averie Cooks’ caramel apple nachos are such a cute idea for a movie night with your kids. They’re ridiculously easy to make and customize with your favorite toppings, but they still feel like an extra-special snack.

Family Fresh Meals is kind of a genius for this hack: Make a simple fresh fruit jam and use it to top a scoop of vanilla ice cream to wow your guests, or just treat yourself. Her recipe is incredibly easy and makes a big batch of jam you can use for all sorts of dishes.

Industry observers note that peach clafoutis is a traditional French dessert, with baked golden edges and a custardy center. A Sweet Thyme’s recipe includes a splash of bourbon and vanilla to deepen the peach flavor, but you’ll be surprised by how easy this showstopper is to make.

With Family Fresh Meals’ recipe, you don’t even have to turn on the oven. You’re literally just whipping together a handful of ingredients, smoothing it into a pie crust, and letting it set in the refrigerator. But nothing makes you feel more like the hostess with the mostest than whipping out a gorgeous pie at the end of dinner.

Recent findings suggest that ina Garten’s viral brownie pudding has a delicious crust with gooey, fudgy goodness underneath. Feel Good Foodie’s version simplifies the ingredient list, and it’s really just a matter of dumping things into a mixer before baking.

BRB while I become known as the strawberry-mascarpone-tart friend...

Industry News: Baking My Nana's Recipes Reminds Me Of The Kind of Mom She Taught Me To Be

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (907 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scarymommy

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The coziness of the holidays gets me all sentimental.
  • Industry observers note that my Nana was not a good cook.
  • It has been revealed that her baking though, now that was good.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The coziness of the holidays gets me all sentimental.

Industry observers note that my Nana was not a good cook. Not really. Her food was always basic. Good, but basic. I know this now that I am grown and trying to figure out if I’m a good cook myself. She was Irish and had about 12 things she knew how to cook and they were basically all holiday menu-specific. She could do up a roast turkey, stuffing, mashed potatoes, gravy. A bag of coleslaw with a bottle of creamy dressing tossed in. She bought those little grocery store dinner rolls and popped them in the oven to warm as my Grandpa carved the turkey, his only chance to shine in the winter season as the barbeque was no longer an option.

It has been revealed that her baking though, now that was good. A bit better than good by ‘80s standards since the Great British Baking Show didn’t exist. She made excellent sticky buns and little donuts she shook in paper bags of cinnamon and sugar while they were piping hot. She baked birthday cakes for all of the grandchildren, chocolate and peanut butter, or strawberry cream, or white cake with jam in the middle.

Most of all, she baked raisin bread. Loaf after loaf of raisin bread for everyone she knew. We’ve never found the recipe in the two decades that she has been gone, and it is the thing her whole family misses the most. The dark, molasses smell of it. A nod to her Nova Scotian heritage. Sturdy enough to toast if you cut your morning slab extra thick. Sturdy enough for a great big smear of peanut butter too. A singular flavor I will miss forever.

Industry observers note that her raisin bread and cinnamon buns and chocolate cakes were not the things that drew us all to her kitchen. Her turkey wasn’t even really moist enough to have us all clamoring for late night sandwiches, and yet there we stood. Every year. Daughters and sons, grandchildren, friends. Some of us in pajamas, others in track pants to accommodate our food babies. My quiet Grandpa hovering around the periphery, hoping someone would make him a plate of food. We came for the sandwich but mostly we came for her. My Nana. A short, bossy, contrary matriarch who made messes, made toast with marmalade on cold mornings, made cup after cup of tea left too long on the stove.

Recent findings suggest that she made me want to be just like her. To call my loves back to my own kitchen. To make people feel welcome and loved and relaxed and just seen, all the time she was seeing us out of the corner of her eye. “What’s wrong?” she’d ask me as she was kneading cinnamon-scented dough for her raisin bread, all casual and relaxed as a viper ready to strike. She knew, she always knew, we came to her kitchen to pray at her feet. To talk out a breakup or a fresh love or a money problem over plates of eggs fried too hard, bread toasted too long. Almost always with a toddler sitting at her feet, a baby on her hip. A smile on her face.

Industry observers note that her technique in the kitchen was really more of a siren song. She chose her smells wisely, I think. She favoured cinnamon over chocolate. Rosemary over garlic. Warm hug smells. Luring us in for a gossip, her favorite appetizer for any meal. Did you hear? Guess who’s dating? You didn’t hear this from me… A buffet of talking and food, of mess and chaos.

It has been 20 years since she died. I am as old as she was when I was a little girl, our golden hour together. And yet, she looms as large now in my holiday kitchen as she did when I was a girl.

It is her voice I hear when I call out to my own sons, “Who’s hungry?” and make us all a major pot of chili to eat while we watch The Lord of the Rings for the hundredth time in the dark quiet of our living room. Or a great stack of buttermilk pancakes to be eaten with overly crisp bacon and real maple syrup, all of us sleepy at our table.

According to recent reports, it was even her voice I heard in my oldest son when he told me he would like to take over Christmas morning breakfast. I sat in the kitchen, a cup of tea at my elbow, as he and his brothers made eggs benedict for all of us. One making artful pour over coffee, another seasoning hashbrowns, still another carefully poaching eggs and adding lemon to his homemade bechamel.

Sources indicate that the food has improved, but the heart of it stays the same. We come back to this kitchen that is not her kitchen but also is her kitchen.

In a recent development, jen McGuire is a contributing writer for Romper and Scary Mommy. She lives in Canada with four boys and teaches life writing workshops where someone cries in every class. When she is not traveling as often as possible, she’s trying to organize pie parties and outdoor karaoke with her neighbors. She will sing Cher’s “If I Could Turn Back Time” at least once, but she’s open to requests.

💡 Key Takeaways
